In all three papers, a large part of the training data is not correct, and checking it more strictly doesn't clearly help. Page numbers below are PDF pages in `llm/post-training/data/`.

**Self-Instruct: 54% of generated examples have all fields valid**
- The authors randomly sampled 200 generated instructions, took one instance for each, and had an expert annotator (one of the authors) judge them (p. 4).
- Results (Table 2, p. 5):
  - 92% of instructions describe a valid task.
  - 79% of inputs are appropriate for the instruction.
  - 58% of outputs are a correct and acceptable response.
  - **54% of examples have all fields valid.**
- So almost half of the sampled examples have at least one flawed field.

**s1: 53.6% of distilled answers are correct**
- The authors keep incorrect distilled generations on purpose, "as we focus on capturing the reasoning process rather than entirely correct solutions" (p. 3).
- Their grader rates **53.6% of s1K as correct**, and 63.0% of the follow-up s1K-1.1 (p. 3).
- The correctness check on the final 1,000 samples used Claude 3.7 as the grader (Appendix C.3, p. 19).

**OpenThoughts: filtering with a GPT verifier didn't help**
- The "GPT Verification" filter asks GPT-4o-mini whether each answer to a question is correct (p. 59).
- In the controlled test, they generated 63,200 answers, applied each filter, then sampled 31,600 question–answer pairs from what was left (p. 9).
- For math, GPT verification scored lower than training without filtering, and lower than random filtering (Table 7, p. 9):

  | Math filter | Average | Math avg |
  |---|---|---|
  | No filtering (63,200 answers, not compute-controlled) | 41.9 | 65.6 |
  | Random filtering | 41.6 | 64.8 |
  | GPT verification | 40.0 | 61.4 |

- For math, random filtering beat every other filtering method. In all domains, training on everything did about as well as any filter. The authors conclude the gains from filtering are not big enough to justify having fewer samples (p. 9).
- One of their main findings is that none of the many verification and answer-filtering methods they tried "gave significant performance improvements" (p. 3).
- An appendix ablation on the earlier OpenThoughts-114K dataset found that verification may hurt at 7B but help at 32B (Table 15, p. 30).
